messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Vignette:
Lan Nguyen was 48 years old, married, and working as a tutor when she came for help, though she described herself as living in a state of near-constant watchfulness that had been present ever since the assault by a former romantic partner years earlier. She had moved through the days then as if trying to keep her balance on uncertain ground, and even now she found herself scanning every place she entered for signs of danger. Lan had been physically abused by a man she had trusted, and the violence had taken place in the private setting of a relationship that should have felt safe. What stayed with her most was not a single clear story she could tell from beginning to end, but a series of disconnected images: a hand, a wall, a doorframe, the look on his face. When she tried to remember the event, she said it was like looking at photographs laid out separately in her mind, each one sharp and frozen but refusing to fit into a coherent sequence. The terror came back with those images in the same raw form as before, so that even thinking about it could make her chest tighten and her stomach drop.

In the months after the abuse, Lan noticed that she was no longer moving through ordinary spaces in the same way. She began checking mirrors repeatedly, not out of vanity but because she needed to know what was behind her and who might be approaching. In shops, parking lots, and hallways, her eyes went immediately to exits, corners, and anything that could be used as a weapon. She would notice bottles, pens, tools, pieces of metal, or heavy objects in any environment and register them almost automatically as potential threats. Walking into a classroom for tutoring sessions, she found herself scanning the room before a student even sat down, taking in chairs, sharp objects, and the position of doors and windows. She described being superalert and watchful without choosing to be, as though her mind and body had become permanently oriented toward danger. At times her body reacted before she had fully registered why she felt tense: her shoulders tightened, her breathing changed, and she would feel a sudden urge to move away or turn around before her thoughts had caught up.

This way of moving through the world also affected how she saw other people. Lan became increasingly vigilant for dangerous people, and she found it hard to settle in crowded places or around strangers whose intentions she could not immediately read. A man standing too close in a grocery line, an unfamiliar person near her car, or someone speaking loudly in a parking lot could all set off the same internal alarm. She had come to believe that you could never really know who might harm you, and that conviction made every new encounter feel uncertain. She did not describe this as a passing fear but as something that had changed how she understood the world and her place in it. She also felt permanently like an outsider now, as though something had happened that separated her from other people in a way she could not undo. Even in familiar company, there was a sense that she was no longer fully part of things, that others moved through life with a kind of ease she could not recover.

Lan’s work as a tutor had gradually become more difficult because it placed her in close contact with new people in private or semi-private settings. She continued to teach because it mattered to her and because she needed the income, but each new student required a silent assessment of the room and the person in it. If a lesson ran late and the building was emptier than usual, she became more uneasy. She often positioned herself near the door or chose seats where she could see the whole room. She avoided lingering afterward, and she watched people’s hands and movements with a seriousness that others sometimes misread as reserve. Over time, the effort of keeping herself alert and appearing composed left her feeling worn down and increasingly separate from those around her, as if she was performing normality from a distance.

What finally brought Lan to seek help was the sense that she could no longer keep managing this level of fear on her own. The checking, the scanning, the startle in her body, and the way memories could arrive in vivid, terror-filled fragments had become exhausting. She was most afraid that she would never feel safe again, that her life had been permanently altered, and that one day she might miss a sign of danger and be harmed before she could react. At the same time, she was hoping for some relief from the constant alertness and for a way to live and work without feeling as though she were always waiting for something terrible to happen.
